Dun describes a color — specifically, a dull, muted, grayish-brown. It sits somewhere between gray and brown, but without the warmth or richness of either. It is flat, faded, and lifeless-looking. Think of it as brown that has had all its energy drained out of it.

If you mixed a muddy brown with a tired gray and let it dry in dim light, you'd get dun.

The easiest way to grasp dun is to feel what it is not:

  • It is not a rich, warm brown (like chocolate or chestnut).
  • It is not a clean, cool gray (like slate or ash).
  • It is not tan or beige — those are lighter and carry warmth.

Dun is heavier and duller than all of these. It is the color of:

  • The coat of a mouse
  • Dry, sun-baked earth after a long drought
  • A donkey's fur
  • Dead grass in late winter
  • Overcast, smoky skies just before rain
  • Parched, desert sand under a cloudy sky

The key feeling the word always carries is dullness and lack of life or brightness. Whenever you see "dun," think: muted, gray-brown, flat, lifeless.

"Dun" is used most often in literary or descriptive writing to paint a picture of bleakness, desolation, or dreariness. When a writer calls a landscape "dun," they are not just describing its color — they are also hinting that it feels barren, bleak, and cheerless.

Some examples:

  • "The soldiers trudged across the dun plains, their boots kicking up pale dust."
    → The landscape is flat, dry, and lifeless.
  • "She wrapped herself in a dun woolen coat and disappeared into the fog."
    → The coat is an unremarkable, grayish-brown — dull, not eye-catching.
  • "The sky had turned dun by afternoon, heavy with unspent rain."
    → The sky is that particular dull, gray-brown of an overcast, oppressive day.
  • "Rolling dun hills stretched away to the horizon with not a tree in sight."
    → The hills are bare, brown-gray, and monotonous.

Notice that in every case, dun brings with it a mood: gloominess, flatness, a lack of cheer. It is rarely used to describe something pleasant or lively.

One of the most classic and precise uses of "dun" is in describing animals — particularly horses. A dun horse has a coat that is a grayish-tan or yellowish-brown, often with a darker stripe running down the middle of its back (called a dorsal stripe) and darker legs. It is an official, recognized coat color in horse breeding, and "dun" is the standard term for it.

You will also hear "dun" used for the coats of:

  • Donkeys (the classic dun animal)
  • Deer (their earthy, muted coats)
  • Mice and rats

In the animal world, dun is essentially the color of natural camouflage — the kind of earth-toned, unremarkable color that helps an animal blend into dry grass and bare ground.

Beyond color, "dun" can also describe a broader quality of dullness or dreariness — not just something that looks gray-brown, but something that feels flat and lifeless. A "dun world" or a "dun existence" might suggest a life without color, excitement, or joy. This usage leans poetic, but it flows naturally from the color's core feeling.
Dun means a dull, muted, grayish-brown color — flat and lifeless, like dry earth, a mouse's fur, or an overcast sky — and it often carries a mood of bleakness or dreariness.

Whenever you want to remember "dun," picture this: a donkey standing on dry, cracked earth under a gray sky. The donkey's coat, the soil, and the sky are all dun — every shade of muted, lifeless gray-brown in one scene.
